newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai crisis ebbs but gloom still seen for bourse.
newsitem.headline: Thai crisis ebbs but gloom still seen for bourse.

text.p: Although the darkest hour may have passed in Thailand's financial crisis, analysts expect more downside as investors realise new government measures aimed at propping up ailing sectors may not address fundamental problems.
"People are beginning to realise the scale of the problem," said Graham Catterwell, head of equities at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "It's not over yet. There is more to come, that's for sure."
Two weeks ago the Thai financial system was rocked by a crisis of confidence, causing the local stock market to plunge to near a five-year low as investors questioned the nation's financial health.

A package of measures, including plans to rescue troubled property developers and their financiers through a multi-billion dollar bond issue, helped restore some confidence to the market, which rebounded last week.
But the recovery appears to be short-lived and the market, which has already lost more than half its value in the past year, looks set to fall further.
In the first sign of what is likely to come in the next few weeks, the Thai bourse took a tumble on Friday, erasing the week's gains as the measures lost their initial shine.
The market fell more than three percent on Friday to end at 694.91 points. Analysts say the fall could continue in the near term and the bourse could drop as low as 580-600 points.
"I feel very sceptical," said one analyst. "I feel that the intervention has brought up sentiment a bit, but I think there will be a bit more downside next week."
Banks and finance counters, which together make up about 40 percent of the market, were the big losers on Friday and that could continue in the next week or so, analysts said.

"We're still underweighting the market," said an analyst at a foreign securities company. "Banks are unattractive, finance companies are unattractive...and banks are the major investment vehicles for foreigners so there's not much left to buy."
Analysts said the market's fall came as investors started to digest the government's measures.

"As usual, people start to pick holes in proposals after they are announced," said George Morgan, country manager for HG Asia. "This news...was a good catalyst to trigger a short-term market rally. But it's not the final solution. They have to deal with some fundametal problems."

The government ordered the country's 15 banks and 91 finance companies -- many of which have broad exposure to the bloated property market -- to boost provisions for sub-standard assets. It also told 10 weakened finance companies to increase capital.
Banks and finance companies have sunk about 800 billion baht ($31 billion) in loans into troubled property firms, many of which are suspected to be bad debts, analysts say.
Although the new measures were welcomed, analysts said finance companies needed a more severe shake-up.

"The government had to do something, but the problem is it is not rewarding well-managed companies and penalising badly- managed ones," said Morgan. "This would have been a good opportunity for a shake-up."
The bond issue to help the property sector is also not addressing a fundamental problem of the sector's over-supply.

"The market should be able to move in the way market forces dictate," said one analyst. "This way it brings more money into the system to inflate demand...but that doesn't get away from the problem that there is still over-supply."
